data.content_ref: inline:{"analogy":null,"claim":"The single dominant cross-city modulator is the sky view factor (SVF): denser, taller building arrays reduce the effective sky view, trapping longwave radiation and slowing nocturnal cooling, so cities with lower mean SVF develop larger nighttime heat islands.","counterconditions":[{"case":"If measurement shows two cities with identical SVF but vastly different nighttime UHI magnitude, SVF alone cannot be the dominant modulator","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If rural and urban SVF differences are small (e.g., very low-density cities) yet nocturnal UHI remains large, the SVF explanation is insufficient","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If longwave trapping effect is quantified and accounts for <30% of the nocturnal cooling-rate difference between city and countryside, SVF is not the single best modulator","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If wind speed variation completely cancels the SVF effect under calm conditions, the mechanism is subordinate to wind dynamics","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"}],"definitions":[],"derivation":[],"formalization_refs":[],"mechanism":"Urban materials with high thermal mass and heat capacity store daytime insolation and release it as sensible heat after sunset. In dense street canyons with low sky view factor, emitted longwave radiation has a high probability of intercepting another building facade rather than escaping to the cold sky. This radiative trapping slows the nocturnal cooling rate, so the stored thermal mass effect persists longer and produces a larger nighttime temperature gap. Cities with deeper, narrower canyons (lower SVF) trap more longwave radiation and thus exhibit larger nocturnal UHI than cities with similar thermal mass but more open geometry.","premises":[],"schema":"deepreason-reasoning-envelope-v1","scope":{"covers":[],"excludes":[]},"simulation_refs":[],"uncertainties":[]}
